sources.title: MSG is back. Is the idea it’s bad for us just a myth or food science?
sources.excerpt: Can MSG cause reactions? A very small percentage of people may have hypersensitivities to MSG.

reasoning: Major scientific and regulatory bodies, including the US Food and Drug Administration (FDA), the World Health Organization (WHO), and the European Food Safety Authority (EFSA), classify monosodium glutamate (MSG) as "generally recognized as safe" (GRAS). Rigorous, double-blind, placebo-controlled studies have consistently failed to establish a causal link between typical dietary consumption of MSG and symptoms like headaches, numbness, or chest pain. The term "Chinese restaurant syndrome" originated from a single anecdotal letter to the New England Journal of Medicine in 1968 and has since been debunked as a myth with xenophobic origins. Furthermore, the glutamate in MSG is chemically identical to the glutamate naturally present in foods like tomatoes, cheese, and mushrooms, which do not produce these symptoms. While a very small subset of the population may exhibit temporary sensitivity to massive doses of MSG consumed without food, MSG does not cause these symptoms under normal eating conditions.
title: MSG causes headaches — 'Chinese restaurant syndrome'
